'''Karl Alexander Müller''' (20 April 1927 – 9 January 2023) was a Swiss [[physicist]]. He received the [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics in 1987 with [[Georg Bednorz]] for their discovery of [[High-temperature superconductivity|superconductivity in ceramic materials]].<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 1987|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1987/summary/|url-status=live|publisher=[[Nobel Foundation]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080919014520/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1987/index.html|archive-date=2008-09-19|access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Karl Alexander Müller was born on 20 April 1927 in [[Basel]], Switzerland, the son of Paul Rudolf Müller and Irma Feigenbaum.<ref name="DHS"/> His mother was [[Jews|Jewish]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jewish Nobel Prize Winners in Physics |url=https://www.jinfo.org/Nobels_Physics.html |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=www.jinfo.org}}</ref> His family immediately moved to [[Salzburg]], Austria, where his father was studying music. Alex and his mother then moved to [[Dornach]], the home of his maternal grandparents. Then they moved to [[Lugano]], in the [[Italian language|Italian]]-speaking part of Switzerland, where he learned to speak Italian fluently. His mother died when he was 11.<ref name="SPS">{{Cite web|title=In Memoriam Karl Alexander Müller|url=https://sps.ch/en/articles/obituaries/karl_alexander_mueller|url-status=live|website=sps.ch|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260508084941/https://sps.ch/en/articles/obituaries/karl_alexander_mueller|archive-date=2026-05-08|access-date=2026-06-21}}</ref>

Müller was sent to school at the Evangelical College in [[Schiers]], in the eastern part of Switzerland. Here he studied from 1938 to 1945, obtaining his baccalaureate (''[[Matura]]''). He then enrolled in the Physics and Mathematics Department of [[ETH Zurich]]. He took courses by [[Wolfgang Pauli]], who made a deep impression on him. After receiving his ''[[Diplom]]'' in 1952,<ref name="DHS"/> he worked for one year, then returned to ETH Zurich for a [[Ph.D.]], submitting his thesis at the end of 1957.<ref name="Nobel bio">{{Cite web|title=K. Alex Müller|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1987/muller/biographical/|url-status=live|publisher=[[Nobel Foundation]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260110083219/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1987/muller/biographical/|archive-date=2026-01-10|access-date=2026-06-21}}</ref>

== Career ==
After graduating in 1958, Müller joined the [[Battelle Memorial Institute]] as the manager of a magnetic resonance group. During this time, he became a lecturer at the [[University of Zürich]]. In 1963, he accepted an offer as a research staff member at the [[IBM Zurich Research Laboratory]] in [[Rüschlikon]], where he remained until his retirement. In parallel, he maintained his affiliation with the University of Zurich, where he was appointed a professor in 1970. He became an [[IBM Fellow]] in 1982.<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

== Research ==
[[File:Karl Alex Muller LANL.jpg|thumb|Müller in 2002]]
For his undergraduate diploma work, Müller studied under G. Busch. He worked on the [[Hall Effect]] in [[tin|gray tin]], a [[semimetal]].

Between his [[undergraduate degree]] and beginning his [[graduate student|graduate studies]], he worked for one year in the Department of Industrial Research at ETH on the [[Eidophor]] large-scale display system.

At [[IBM]] his research for almost 15 years centered on SrTiO<sub>3</sub> ([[strontium titanate]]) and related [[perovskite]] compounds. He studied their [[photochromism|photochromic]] properties when doped with various [[transition metal|transition-metal]] [[ion]]s; their [[chemical bond|chemical binding]], [[ferroelectricity|ferroelectric]] and soft-mode properties; and the critical and multicritical phenomena of their structural [[phase transition]]s. Important highlights of this research have been published in a book written together with [[Tom Kool]] from the [[University of Amsterdam]] (publisher: [[World Scientific]]).

== Personal life and death ==
In the spring of 1956, Müller married Ingeborg Marie Louise Winkler. They had a son, Eric, in the summer of 1957, and a daughter, Sylvia, in 1960.<ref name="DHS">''[http://www.hls-dhs-dss.ch/textes/f/F31540.php Dictionnaire Historique de la Suisse]'' (19 Nov 2009).</ref>

Müller died on 9 January 2023 in [[Zurich]] at the age of 95.<ref>[https://www.news.uzh.ch/de/articles/news/2023/Alex_M%C3%BCller.html ''Gegen den Strom schwimmen.''] In: ''[[Universität Zürich]]'', 17 January 2023.</ref><ref>[https://www.swissinfo.ch/ger/alle-news-in-kuerze/physik-nobelpreistraeger-karl-alex-mueller-stirbt-mit-95-jahren/48209386 ''Physik Nobelpreisträger Karl Alex Müller stirbt mit 95 Jahren.''] In: Swissinfo.ch, 17 January 2023.</ref>

== Nobel Prize-winning work ==
{{Main|High-temperature superconductivity}}
In the early 1980s, Müller began searching for substances that would become superconductive at higher temperatures. The highest [[superconductivity|critical temperature]] (''T''<sub>c</sub>) attainable at that time was about 23 [[Kelvin|K]]. In 1983 Müller recruited Georg Bednorz to IBM, to help systematically test various oxides. A few recent studies had indicated these materials might superconduct, but experts who knew about Müller's idea thought it was “crazy”.<ref>Holton, Gerald. ''The Scientific Imagination'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=BMe_IgVtk90C&pg=PR25 p. xxv] (Harvard University Press, 1998).</ref> In 1986 the two researchers succeeded in achieving superconductivity in [[lanthanum barium copper oxide]] (LBCO) at a temperature of 35 [[kelvin|K]]. Over the previous 75 years the critical temperature had risen from 11 K in 1911 to 23 [[Kelvin|K]] in 1973 where it had remained for 13 years. Thus 35 K was incredibly high by the prevailing standards of superconductivity research. This discovery stimulated a great deal of additional research in [[high-temperature superconductivity]], leading to the discovery of compounds such as [[BSCCO]] (''T''<sub>c</sub>&nbsp;= 107 K) and [[YBCO]] (''T'''<sub>c</sub>&nbsp;= 92 K).

They reported their discovery in the June 1986 issue of ''[[Zeitschrift für Physik B]]''.<ref>{{cite journal| author = J. G. Bednorz and K. A. Müller| title = Possible high T<sub>c</sub> superconductivity in the Ba−La−Cu−O system| journal = Z. Phys. B| volume = 64| year = 1986| pages = 189–193| doi = 10.1007/BF01303701| issue = 1|bibcode = 1986ZPhyB..64..189B | s2cid = 118314311}}</ref> Before the end of the year, [[Shoji Tanaka]] at the [[University of Tokyo]] and then [[Paul C. W. Chu|Paul Chu]] at the [[University of Houston]] had each independently confirmed their result. A couple of months later Chu achieved superconductivity at 93 K in [[YBCO]], triggering a stampede of scientific interest exemplified by the 1987 "[[Woodstock of physics]]", at which Müller was a featured presenter.<ref name = "Chang">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/03/06/science/06supe.html|title=Physicists Remember When Superconductors Were Hot|last=Chang|first=Kenneth|date=6 March 2007|work=New York Times|access-date=22 August 2013}}</ref>

In 1987, Müller and Bednorz were jointly awarded the [[Nobel Prize]] in physics—the shortest time between the discovery and the prize award for any scientific Nobel.
